questions.title: Modules & Imports practice 1
questions.prompt: Which line makes the `random` module available under its own name?
choices: import random
from random import randint
include random
using random
questions.explanation: `import random` binds the module name. Its functions are then reached with a dot, such as `random.randint(1, 6)`.

questions.title: Modules & Imports practice 2
choices: When this file is run directly
Every time the file is imported
Only after an error
Before Python reads the file
questions.explanation: Python sets `__name__` to `"__main__"` for the file that starts the program. Imported modules receive their module names instead.

questions.title: Trace Modules & Imports
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: Importing the module keeps the source of `sqrt` clear. The dot says that the function comes from math. The resulting output is '5.0'.

questions.title: Modules & Imports practice 5
questions.prompt: Why prefer `import math; math.sqrt(16)` over `from math import *`?
choices: The wildcard dumps every name in and can quietly overwrite one you defined
The wildcard import is a syntax error
math.sqrt is faster than sqrt
sqrt does not exist in the math module
questions.explanation: `from math import *` pulls in every public name at once, which hides where a name came from and can shadow something you already defined (for example, your own `sqrt`). `import math` keeps the boundary visible: `math.sqrt` says exactly where it lives. Both call the same function at the same speed.

questions.title: Modules & Imports concept check 1
questions.prompt: What happens to top-level Python statements when a file is imported?
choices: Statements at the top level run when Python imports the file. Place demo code and direct user input inside a main guard so importing the module does not start them.
Put input prompts at top level so importing starts interaction.
Use wildcard imports so every name appears from nowhere.
Split code into files without a clear responsibility.
questions.explanation: Statements at the top level run when Python imports the file. Place demo code and direct user input inside a main guard so importing the module does not start them. This matters because import code should make dependencies clear without running surprising work during import.

questions.title: Modules & Imports concept check 2
questions.prompt: Which choice describes a reliable Modules & Imports practice?
choices: Name a file the same as a standard library module.
Group code by one clear purpose.
Import a module only for one hidden side effect.
Keep demo code outside a main guard.
questions.explanation: Group code by one clear purpose. This matters because import code should make dependencies clear without running surprising work during import.

questions.title: Modules & Imports concept check 3
questions.prompt: Which Modules & Imports code review note is accurate?
choices: Duplicate the same helper in several files.
Use relative imports without checking the package structure.
Prefer imports that show where a name came from.
Assume importing a file never runs any code.
questions.explanation: Prefer imports that show where a name came from. This matters because import code should make dependencies clear without running surprising work during import.

questions.title: Modules & Imports concept check 4
questions.prompt: Which Modules & Imports habit prevents a common mistake?
choices: Expose every internal helper as part of the module contract.
Use a module name that hides what it contains.
Make modules depend on each other in a cycle.
Avoid wildcard imports.
questions.explanation: Avoid wildcard imports. This matters because import code should make dependencies clear without running surprising work during import.

questions.title: Modules & Imports concept check 5
questions.prompt: Which Modules & Imports advice is accurate?
choices: Keep top-level work small.
Reload modules to reset ordinary program state.
Use import order to control unrelated behavior.
Ignore where a name came from during review.
questions.explanation: Keep top-level work small. This matters because import code should make dependencies clear without running surprising work during import.

questions.title: Modules & Imports concept check 6
questions.prompt: Which Modules & Imports reasoning is accurate?
choices: Put tests and production code in one mixed block.
Put demos and command-line input behind a main guard.
Use a module when a simple local function is enough.
Depend on the current working directory instead of package paths.
questions.explanation: Put demos and command-line input behind a main guard. This matters because import code should make dependencies clear without running surprising work during import.
